opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most important questions for universities right now, and honestly, there's been a lot of soul-searching about it. If you look at the last few years, the frontier of foundation models has clearly shifted to industry. Training a state-of-the-art large model today takes tens of thousands of GPUs, hundreds of millions of dollars, sometimes more, plus enormous data pipelines and engineering teams. No university in the world, not Tsinghua, not Stanford, not MIT, can compete head-to-head on that kind of scale. So I don't think the university's role is to build the biggest model and race OpenAI or Google or the leading Chinese companies on parameter count.

But that doesn't mean universities are irrelevant. Quite the opposite. I see three or four roles that are actually more important than ever.

The first is fundamental research, the things companies don't have the patience or incentive to do. Companies are optimizing for the next product cycle, the next benchmark, the next release. Universities can ask the harder, longer-term questions: Are transformers and scaling laws really the end game? What comes after next-token prediction? How do we get true reasoning, causality, efficient learning with much less data and energy? Many of the breakthroughs we now take for granted, deep learning itself, reinforcement learning, even the attention mechanism, have roots in academic work. The next paradigm shift is just as likely to come from a small lab with a bold idea as from a giant compute cluster.

The second is talent. Universities are where the people come from. Almost every key person in today's leading AI companies came through a university lab. At Tsinghua's Institute for AI Industry Research, AIR, we think a lot about how to train students who understand both the science and the real-world problems, people who can move between academia and industry.

The third area is what I'd call the "vertical" and the "edge." Instead of general-purpose giant models, universities can do very well on domain-specific models, for example AI for life sciences, drug discovery, biology, healthcare, and also embodied AI, robotics, autonomous driving. These areas need deep domain knowledge, interdisciplinary collaboration, and trust, and universities are good at that. We did work on a biomedical foundation model, and in autonomous driving with open-source platforms, for exactly this reason. Small, efficient models running on devices are another area where academia can lead, because the constraint is cleverness, not compute.

And the fourth is being a neutral, trusted voice on safety, governance, and evaluation. As these models become more powerful, someone has to independently measure their risks, their biases, their alignment. Companies have conflicts of interest. Universities can be the honest broker, help set standards, and engage internationally, including between China and the US, even when the geopolitics is difficult.

So the model I believe in is collaboration, not competition. Companies bring compute, data, and engineering scale. Universities bring original ideas, talent, and independence. At AIR we deliberately structured ourselves this way: we work closely with industry partners, sometimes they provide the compute, we provide the research, and the results often go open source so the whole ecosystem benefits. I think that's the healthiest relationship. If universities try to become mini-companies, they lose what makes them special. If they ignore industry completely, they become irrelevant. The sweet spot is in between.

r001.rationale: The response says companies bring compute, data, and engineering scale, and describes partners providing compute for university research.

r002.rationale: It says industry leads in scale and suggests a future paradigm shift may come from academic research; it does not characterize development as scaling existing advances rather than creating fundamentally new ones.

r003.rationale: It mentions engineering teams and fundamental research, but does not say engineering innovation is more prevalent than algorithmic innovation.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that universities should not try to compete with companies on the frontier of scale. That race is about compute, data, and capital, and a university will never have the GPU budget of a big tech firm. At AIR at Tsinghua, we made that decision early. We are not going to train the biggest general-purpose model. It would be a waste of our resources and our talent.

What a university can do, and should do, is three things.

First, foundational research on the questions companies don't have time for. Why do these models work? What are the limits of scaling? How do we make them more efficient, more interpretable, more trustworthy? Companies are under enormous commercial pressure, so they optimize for the next product cycle. A university can look five or ten years out. Many of the key ideas behind today's models came out of academic labs long before they were commercially useful.

Second, vertical models in domains where companies have less incentive but society has real need. We work on autonomous driving, biology and healthcare, green computing. In these areas a smaller, specialized model trained with domain data and physical constraints can be more valuable than a huge general model. The university also has an advantage here because we can collaborate across disciplines, with hospitals, with biologists, in a way that is hard inside one company.

Third, and maybe most important, talent. The people building foundation models at every major company were trained at universities. If we stop training students at the frontier, in a few years there will be no one to build the next generation. So we need enough compute to let students touch real models, even if we can't train the largest ones.

And I think the relationship should be collaboration, not competition. Companies have scale and real-world data. Universities have openness and long time horizons. The best outcomes come when a company open-sources a model and the university community studies it, improves it, and sends back both ideas and people. That's the model I would like to see in China, and it's largely how it has worked in the U.S. as well.

r001.rationale: The response says companies bring scale and real-world data, and describes collaboration and open-sourced models as ways universities can study and improve them.

r002.rationale: It discusses scaling and foundational research, but does not characterize the main innovation as scaling existing advances rather than creating fundamentally new ones.

r003.rationale: It does not compare engineering innovation with algorithmic innovation or say engineering innovation is more prevalent.

astra-6.text:
I think universities and companies have complementary roles. Companies have the computing resources, the data, and the engineering teams to build large models and bring them into products. A university does not necessarily need to compete by building an even bigger model.

Our role is to explore the questions that may take longer to answer: Can we develop a different architecture? Can we make models learn more efficiently, reason more reliably, and operate safely? Universities also have a responsibility to educate people who can understand these systems deeply and challenge the assumptions behind them.

But you do need to build things. If you only discuss foundation models in theory, you miss many of the important research problems. So I would encourage universities to build models at a scale that supports their research, collaborate with industry, and choose areas where they can make a distinctive contribution. The goal is to create new knowledge and new possibilities.

r001.rationale: The response says companies have computing, data, and engineering resources and recommends collaborating with industry, but does not clearly describe collaboration as the way universities gain access to those resources.

r002.rationale: The response does not characterize development as mainly scaling existing advances; it instead raises exploring different architectures and other research questions.

r003.rationale: The response mentions companies’ engineering teams and university research, but does not say engineering innovation is more prevalent than algorithmic innovation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think universities and companies have complementary roles. Companies have the computing resources, engineering teams, and access to real applications needed to train and deploy large foundation models. A university should ask where it can make a distinctive contribution, rather than simply compete to build a bigger model.

For universities, that means exploring fundamental questions, trying approaches that may not have an immediate commercial return, and training people who can move the field forward. It also means studying how to make models more reliable, efficient, and understandable.

There is a strong opportunity to work together. Companies can provide infrastructure and practical problems, while universities contribute new ideas and independent research. The university’s success should be measured by the knowledge and talent it creates, as well as by the models it builds.

r001.rationale: It explicitly describes companies providing infrastructure and practical problems while universities contribute research, indicating collaboration gives universities access to resources relevant to model development.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize the main innovation as scaling existing advances rather than creating fundamentally new ones.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the prevalence of engineering innovation with algorithmic innovation.
